lessons.title: Rates of Reaction and Collision Theory
lessons.description: Measuring and calculating reaction rates, the factors that affect them, and collision theory.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Rate of Reaction?

The rate of reaction tells us how fast a chemical reaction happens. Some reactions are very fast — like an explosion or the neutralisation of an acid. Others are very slow, such as rusting or the weathering of rocks. In GCSE Chemistry, you need to know how to measure, calculate, and explain what controls the rate of a reaction.

Rate of reaction can be defined as the amount of product formed, or the amount of reactant used up, per unit of time. The equation is:

Key Fact

\(Rate \text{of reaction} = \text{amount of product formed} \div time\) — or — \(\text{amount of reactant used up} \div time\). The units depend on what you measure: g/s if you measure mass, or cm³/s if you measure the volume of gas produced.

Measuring Rate of Reaction

There are two main practical methods for measuring rate of reaction at GCSE. Both appear in the AQA required practicals and you need to know the advantages and limitations of each.

When a reaction produces a gas, you can collect and measure the gas using a gas syringe or by collecting the gas over water using an inverted measuring cylinder. You record the volume of gas at regular time intervals (e.g. every 10 seconds) and plot a graph of volume against time.

Example: Marble chips (calcium carbonate) reacting with hydrochloric acid: CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2. The carbon dioxide gas is collected in the gas syringe. The faster the syringe plunger moves out, the faster the reaction.

Place the reaction flask on a balance and record the mass at regular time intervals. As gas escapes from the flask, the mass decreases. You plot a graph of mass lost against time. This method works well for reactions that produce carbon dioxide or hydrogen gas.

Advantage: Easy to set up and gives continuous data. Disadvantage: Gas escapes into the room, so the mass readings are slightly less accurate than collecting the gas directly. Very light gases like hydrogen are hard to detect by mass loss.

Reading Rate from a Graph

When you plot a graph of product formed (or reactant used up) against time, the gradient (steepness) of the line tells you the rate. A steep line means a fast reaction. A shallow line means a slow reaction. When the line goes flat, the reaction has finished — one of the reactants has been completely used up.

To calculate the rate at a specific point on a curved graph, draw a tangent to the curve at that point and find the gradient of the tangent. The gradient equals the change in the y-axis divided by the change in the x-axis.

Key Fact

\(Gradient = \text{change in} y \div \text{change in} x.\) On a volume–time graph, this gives rate in cm³/s. On a mass-loss graph, it gives rate in g/s. The mean rate for the whole reaction is the total product formed divided by the total time taken.

Collision Theory

Collision theory explains why reactions happen at different rates. For a reaction to occur, the reacting particles must collide with each other. But not every collision leads to a reaction — two conditions must be met:

1. The particles must collide with enough energy. The minimum energy needed for a collision to result in a reaction is called the activation energy. If particles collide with less energy than this, they just bounce apart. 2. The particles must collide in the correct orientation — they need to hit each other the right way round so that bonds can break and new bonds can form.

Anything that increases the frequency of successful collisions will increase the rate of reaction. The four main factors that do this are temperature, concentration, surface area, and catalysts.

Factors Affecting Rate

Temperature

Increasing the temperature makes particles move faster because they have more kinetic energy. This has two effects: particles collide more often (higher collision frequency), and a greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy. Both effects increase the rate. This is why reactions are usually faster when heated.

Concentration (and Pressure for Gases)

Increasing the concentration of a solution means there are more reactant particles in the same volume. This increases the frequency of collisions, so the rate increases. For gaseous reactions, increasing the pressure has the same effect — it forces particles closer together so they collide more often.

Surface Area

Breaking a solid into smaller pieces increases its surface area. More surface is exposed to the other reactant, so more collisions can happen at the same time. For example, powdered marble chips react much faster with hydrochloric acid than large lumps because the powder has a much greater surface area.

Key Fact

All four factors — temperature, concentration, surface area, and catalysts — affect rate by changing the frequency or energy of collisions. In every exam answer, link back to collision theory: more frequent collisions or more energetic collisions means a faster rate.

Catalysts

A catalyst is a substance that increases the rate of a reaction without being used up. It works by providing an alternative reaction pathway that has a lower activation energy. This means a greater proportion of collisions now have enough energy to react, so the rate increases. The catalyst is chemically unchanged at the end — it can be reused.

Enzymes are biological catalysts that control reactions in living organisms. In industry, catalysts are used to reduce energy costs — reactions can run at lower temperatures, saving fuel and money. Different reactions require different catalysts.

AQA’s required practical investigates how changing one factor (e.g. concentration of acid or size of marble chips) affects the rate of reaction between marble chips and dilute hydrochloric acid. You measure the volume of CO2 produced using a gas syringe and record it at regular intervals.

Key points: Use the same mass of marble chips and the same volume of acid each time (control variables). Change only the independent variable (e.g. concentration). Repeat each test at least three times and calculate a mean. Plot the results on a graph — steeper curves mean faster reactions.

Common error: Students often forget that although the rate changes, the total volume of gas produced stays the same (when excess acid is used) because the same mass of marble chips is always used. The reaction just finishes sooner at higher concentrations or temperatures.

When two curves are plotted on the same axes, the steeper curve represents the faster reaction. If both curves reach the same final volume, the same amount of reactant was used — the reaction just finished sooner. If one curve reaches a lower final volume, less gas was produced (e.g. less reactant was used). Be ready to explain these differences using collision theory.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about rate of reaction, always link your explanation to collision theory. Simply saying “the reaction is faster because there are more collisions” is not enough — you must explain why collisions are more frequent or more energetic. For example: “Increasing temperature gives particles more kinetic energy, so they move faster, collide more frequently, and a greater proportion of collisions exceed the activation energy.” In calculate questions, remember to include units (g/s or cm³/s) and show your working clearly.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Rate of reaction = amount of product formed ÷ time. Measure it using a gas syringe (volume of gas) or a balance (mass lost).
  • Collision theory: reactions only happen when particles collide with sufficient energy (the activation energy) and the correct orientation.
  • Four factors increase rate — higher temperature, higher concentration (or pressure), greater surface area, and catalysts — all by increasing the frequency or energy of collisions.

lessons.title: Reversible Reactions and Equilibrium
lessons.description: Reversible reactions, dynamic equilibrium, and how changing conditions shifts the balance.
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Reversible Reaction?

Most chemical reactions you have studied so far go in one direction — reactants turn into products and the reaction stops. But some reactions can go in both directions. In a reversible reaction, the products can react to reform the original reactants. We show this using the equilibrium symbol ⇌ instead of a normal arrow.

A classic example is the thermal decomposition of ammonium chloride. When heated, ammonium chloride (a white solid) breaks down into ammonia and hydrogen chloride — two colourless gases. When these gases cool and meet, they recombine to form ammonium chloride again:

\(\text{ammonium chloride} \rightleftharpoons ammonia + \text{hydrogen chloride}\)
NH4Cl(s) ⇌ NH3(g) + HCl(g)

You can see this in action: when you heat ammonium chloride in a test tube, a white solid forms higher up in the tube where the gases have cooled and recombined. This proves the reaction is reversible.

Key Fact

The ⇌ symbol tells you a reaction is reversible. A normal arrow (→) means the reaction only goes one way. Never use a normal arrow for a reversible reaction in the exam.

Hydrated Copper Sulfate — Another Reversible Reaction

Another important example is the hydration of copper sulfate. Hydrated copper sulfate is a blue crystalline solid. When you heat it, it loses its water of crystallisation and turns into a white powder called anhydrous copper sulfate:

\(\text{hydrated copper sulfate} (blue) \rightleftharpoons \text{anhydrous copper sulfate} (white) + water\)
CuSO4·5H2O(s) ⇌ CuSO4(s) + 5H2O(l)

If you add water back to the white anhydrous powder, it turns blue again and gets hot — the reverse reaction is exothermic. This colour change is so reliable that anhydrous copper sulfate is used as a chemical test for the presence of water.

To test for the presence of water, add the liquid to white anhydrous copper sulfate. If the powder turns blue, water is present. This does not tell you the water is pure — to confirm pure water, check the boiling point (100 °C at standard pressure). Cobalt chloride paper can also be used: it turns from blue to pink when water is present.

Energy Changes in Reversible Reactions

In any reversible reaction, if the forward reaction is exothermic (gives out energy), then the reverse reaction is endothermic (takes in energy) — and vice versa. The amount of energy transferred in each direction is exactly the same.

For the copper sulfate example: the forward reaction (heating blue copper sulfate to drive off water) is endothermic — you have to supply heat energy. The reverse reaction (adding water to the white powder) is exothermic — the mixture gets hot. The energy released going one way equals the energy absorbed going the other way.

Key Fact

If a reversible reaction is exothermic in the forward direction, it is endothermic in the reverse direction — and the energy change is the same in both directions. This is a common exam question.

Dynamic Equilibrium

When a reversible reaction takes place in a closed system (where nothing can get in or out), something interesting happens. At first the forward reaction is fast because there are lots of reactants. As products build up, the reverse reaction speeds up. Eventually, the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction. This is called dynamic equilibrium.

“Dynamic” means that both reactions are still happening — molecules are constantly reacting in both directions. “Equilibrium” means the overall concentrations of reactants and products stay the same because the two rates are balanced. It is not a static situation where everything has stopped.

Key Fact

Dynamic equilibrium requires a closed system. The forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so concentrations of reactants and products do not change — but the reaction has not stopped.

Le Châtelier’s Principle

Le Châtelier’s principle states that if a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change in conditions, the position of equilibrium shifts to partially oppose that change. In other words, the system tries to “undo” whatever you did to it. This principle lets you predict which way the equilibrium will shift when you change temperature, pressure, or concentration.

If you increase the temperature, the equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction to absorb the extra heat. If you decrease the temperature, the equilibrium shifts in the exothermic direction to release heat and restore the temperature. Changing temperature changes both the rate and the position of equilibrium — and therefore changes the yield of products.

Example: In a reversible reaction where the forward reaction is exothermic, increasing the temperature will favour the reverse (endothermic) reaction, producing more reactants and fewer products. The yield of products decreases.

For reactions involving gases, changing the pressure affects the equilibrium position. If you increase the pressure, the equilibrium shifts towards the side with fewer moles of gas — this reduces the pressure. If you decrease the pressure, the equilibrium shifts towards the side with more moles of gas.

Example: Consider N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g). The left side has 4 moles of gas (1 + 3) and the right side has 2. Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right, producing more ammonia.

If you increase the concentration of a reactant, the equilibrium shifts to the right (forward direction) to use up the extra reactant, producing more products. If you increase the concentration of a product, the equilibrium shifts to the left (reverse direction) to use up the extra product.

Example: In the reaction A + B ⇌ C + D, adding more of substance A shifts the equilibrium to the right, increasing the yield of C and D until a new equilibrium is established.

Catalysts and Equilibrium

A catalyst speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally. This means a catalyst helps the system reach equilibrium faster, but it does not change the position of equilibrium or the yield of products. The same amounts of reactants and products are present at equilibrium whether a catalyst is used or not — you just get there more quickly.

Applying Equilibrium: The Haber Process

The Haber process is a real-world application of equilibrium principles. Nitrogen from the air reacts with hydrogen (from natural gas) to produce ammonia:

\(N_{2}(g) + 3H_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_{3}(g)\) — the forward reaction is exothermic.

Using Le Châtelier’s principle: a low temperature and high pressure would give the best yield of ammonia. However, low temperatures make the reaction too slow, so a compromise temperature of about 450 °C is used. High pressure (around 200 atmospheres) favours ammonia production. An iron catalyst is used to speed up the reaction without changing the yield. Any unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled back through the reactor.

Key Fact

The Haber process uses a compromise temperature (about 450 °C), high pressure (200 atm), and an iron catalyst. High pressure increases yield; the moderate temperature balances acceptable yield with a reasonable rate of reaction.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions on equilibrium, always state the direction of the shift AND explain why using Le Châtelier’s principle. For example: “Increasing temperature shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic direction because the system acts to absorb the extra heat energy.” Simply saying “it shifts right” without the reasoning will not earn full marks. In 6-mark extended response questions, use a specific example like the Haber process to illustrate your points.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Reversible reactions go in both directions (shown by ⇌). If the forward reaction is exothermic, the reverse is endothermic by the same amount of energy.
  • Dynamic equilibrium occurs in a closed system when the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal — concentrations stay constant but the reaction has not stopped.
  • Le Châtelier’s principle: changing temperature, pressure, or concentration shifts the equilibrium to partially oppose the change. Catalysts speed up both directions equally and do not change the position of equilibrium.

practice_questions.text: The Haber process uses a temperature of about 450°C and a pressure of 200 atmospheres. The forward reaction (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃) is exothermic. Compare and explain the effect of using a lower temperature versus a higher pressure on the yield of ammonia.

Award up to 4 marks:
• Lower temperature shifts equilibrium to the exothermic (forward) direction, increasing ammonia yield (1)
• However, lower temperature decreases the rate of reaction, so less ammonia is produced per unit time (1)
• Higher pressure shifts equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas (right side / 2 moles vs 4 moles), increasing ammonia yield (1)
• A compromise temperature of 450°C is used to balance yield and rate; high pressure (200 atm) is used because it increases both yield and rate (1)

practice_questions.text: A reversible reaction reaches dynamic equilibrium in a closed system. The forward reaction is endothermic. Explain what would happen to the position of equilibrium and the yield of products if: (a) the temperature is increased; (b) a catalyst is added.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed, logically structured answer covering both parts with correct application of Le Châtelier’s principle. E.g. (a) Increasing temperature adds energy to the system. Le Châtelier’s principle states the equilibrium will shift to oppose the change — it shifts in the endothermic direction (the forward direction) to absorb the extra energy. This increases the yield of products. (b) A catalyst speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally. The system reaches equilibrium faster, but the position of equilibrium does not change — the yield of products remains the same.
Mid band (3-4): Correct identification of shifts for both parts but limited explanation of why, or one part fully explained and one part incomplete.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statements about equilibrium shifting, limited use of Le Châtelier’s principle, may contain errors or only address one part.

lessons.title: Crude Oil, Hydrocarbons and Cracking
lessons.description: Fractional distillation of crude oil, hydrocarbon properties, and why cracking matters.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Crude Oil?

Crude oil is a finite resource found trapped in rocks beneath the Earth’s surface. It formed over millions of years from the remains of ancient plants and tiny sea creatures that were buried under layers of sediment. Heat and pressure gradually transformed this biological material into a complex mixture of hydrocarbons — compounds containing only hydrogen and carbon atoms.

Crude oil is not a single substance. It is a mixture of many different hydrocarbons, each with a different chain length and boiling point. Because they are not chemically bonded together, they can be separated using physical methods. This is what makes crude oil so useful — it can be split into groups of similar molecules called fractions, each with different properties and uses.

Key Fact

Crude oil is a finite (non-renewable) resource. It is a mixture of hydrocarbons — compounds containing only hydrogen and carbon atoms. These hydrocarbons can be separated because they have different boiling points.

Alkanes — The Simplest Hydrocarbons

The main type of hydrocarbon found in crude oil is the alkane. Alkanes are called saturated hydrocarbons because they contain only single covalent bonds between carbon atoms — every carbon atom forms as many bonds to hydrogen as possible.

Alkanes follow a general formula: \(C_{n}H_{2n+2}\). This means if you know how many carbon atoms are in the chain, you can work out the number of hydrogen atoms. The first four alkanes are:

C1

Methane (CH4)

One carbon, four hydrogens. The main component of natural gas.

C2

Ethane (C2H6)

Two carbons, six hydrogens. Found in natural gas.

C3

Propane (C3H8)

Three carbons, eight hydrogens. Used as camping gas and heating fuel.

C4

Butane (C4H10)

Four carbons, ten hydrogens. Used in cigarette lighters and portable stoves.

How Chain Length Affects Properties

The length of a hydrocarbon chain determines its physical properties. As the number of carbon atoms increases, the intermolecular forces between molecules get stronger. This means longer chains require more energy to separate, which directly affects boiling point, viscosity, and flammability.

Key Fact

As hydrocarbon chain length increases: boiling point increases, viscosity increases (thicker, harder to pour), and flammability decreases (harder to ignite). Short-chain hydrocarbons are runny, easy to light, and have low boiling points.

Think of it this way: petrol (short chains) flows easily and catches fire with a spark, while bitumen (very long chains) is thick like tar, does not flow, and is difficult to ignite. This pattern of properties determines what each fraction is used for.

Fractional Distillation

Fractional distillation is the industrial process used to separate crude oil into useful fractions. It works because the different hydrocarbons in crude oil have different boiling points, and a mixture of liquids can be separated if they boil at different temperatures.

The process follows a clear sequence. First, crude oil is heated in a furnace until it vaporises. The hot vapour is then fed into the bottom of a tall fractionating column. The column is very hot at the bottom (around 350°C) and cooler at the top (around 25°C).

As the vapour rises up the column, it gradually cools. When a hydrocarbon vapour reaches the height where the temperature matches its boiling point, it condenses back into a liquid and is collected. Short-chain hydrocarbons have low boiling points, so they rise to the top before condensing. Long-chain hydrocarbons have high boiling points, so they condense near the bottom.

The result is that crude oil is separated into several fractions: gases at the top (used as fuels like LPG), then petrol, kerosene (jet fuel), diesel, fuel oil, and finally bitumen at the very bottom (used for road surfaces). Each fraction is a mixture of hydrocarbons with similar boiling points and chain lengths.

Combustion of Hydrocarbons

Hydrocarbons are extremely useful as fuels because they release large amounts of energy when burned. When a hydrocarbon burns completely in plenty of oxygen, the products are carbon dioxide and water. This is called complete combustion.

For example, propane burns completely: \(C_{3}H_{8} + 5O_{2} \rightarrow 3CO_{2} + 4H_{2}O\)

However, if there is not enough oxygen, incomplete combustion occurs. This produces toxic carbon monoxide (CO) instead of carbon dioxide, and may also produce carbon particulates (soot). Carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless gas that is extremely dangerous because it binds to haemoglobin in the blood, preventing oxygen transport.

Key Fact

Complete combustion (plenty of O2): hydrocarbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. Incomplete combustion (limited O2): produces carbon monoxide (toxic) and/or carbon particulates (soot), which cause global dimming.

Why Is Cracking Needed?

Cracking is a thermal decomposition reaction that breaks long-chain hydrocarbons into shorter, more useful ones. The demand for different fractions is not equal — there is far greater demand for short-chain hydrocarbons (like petrol and gases) than for the long-chain fractions (like fuel oil and bitumen) that make up a large proportion of crude oil.

Cracking solves this supply-and-demand problem. It converts the excess long-chain fractions into the shorter-chain molecules that are in high demand, making the refining process much more economically efficient.

Catalytic cracking: Long-chain hydrocarbons are heated until they vaporise, then passed over a hot catalyst (typically a zeolite catalyst at about 600–700°C). This breaks the molecules into shorter alkanes and alkenes.

Steam cracking: Long-chain hydrocarbons are mixed with steam and heated to very high temperatures (over 800°C). This also produces shorter alkanes and alkenes. Steam cracking tends to produce a higher proportion of alkenes.

In both methods, the key products are shorter-chain alkanes (useful as fuels) and alkenes (useful as petrochemicals — the starting materials for making plastics, solvents, and detergents).

Cracking produces alkenes as well as alkanes. Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons — they contain a carbon–carbon double bond (C=C). Their general formula is \(C_{n}H_{2n}\). The simplest alkene is ethene (C2H4), which is the starting material for making poly(ethene), the most common plastic.

You can distinguish alkenes from alkanes using the bromine water test. When bromine water (which is orange) is added to an alkene, it decolourises (turns colourless) because the bromine reacts with the double bond. With an alkane, bromine water stays orange because there is no double bond to react with.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about fractional distillation, always link the chain length to the property being asked about — explain why boiling point increases (stronger intermolecular forces between longer chains) rather than just stating the trend. For cracking questions, make sure you state that cracking produces alkenes as well as shorter alkanes — a common mistake is forgetting the alkenes. If asked to compare alkanes and alkenes, mention that alkenes are unsaturated (contain a C=C double bond) and can be tested with bromine water.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Crude oil is a finite mixture of hydrocarbons separated by fractional distillation based on different boiling points — short chains rise to the top, long chains stay at the bottom.
  • As chain length increases, boiling point and viscosity increase while flammability decreases — these trends are caused by stronger intermolecular forces.
  • Cracking breaks long-chain hydrocarbons into shorter alkanes (fuels) and alkenes (for making plastics), solving the mismatch between supply and demand.

lessons.title: Chemical Analysis: Purity, Chromatography and Gas Tests
lessons.description: How to test for pure substances, separate mixtures using chromatography, and identify common gases.
lessons.content_html:
Pure Substances in Chemistry

In everyday language, “pure” means natural or uncontaminated — like “pure orange juice.” But in chemistry, the word has a very specific meaning. A pure substance contains only a single element or a single compound. Pure water, for example, contains nothing but H2O molecules. Crude oil is not pure because it is a mixture of many different hydrocarbons.

Key Fact

A pure substance has a sharp melting point and a sharp boiling point. An impure substance melts and boils over a range of temperatures. Impurities lower the melting point and raise the boiling point. For example, pure water melts at exactly 0°C and boils at exactly 100°C, but seawater (which contains dissolved salt) melts below 0°C.

This means that if you measure the melting point of an unknown white powder and find it melts sharply at one temperature, it is likely pure. If it melts gradually over a range of temperatures, it is a mixture.

Formulations

A formulation is a special type of mixture. The components are mixed in carefully measured quantities so that the final product has exactly the right properties for its purpose. Unlike a random mixture, each ingredient in a formulation serves a specific function.

Formulations are everywhere in daily life. Medicines contain an active ingredient plus binders, coatings, and flavourings. Paints are formulations of pigment, solvent, binder, and additives. Other examples include cleaning products, fuels, cosmetics, fertilisers, and alloys. Each component is present in a precise proportion — too much or too little of any ingredient would change the product’s properties.

Medicine: A paracetamol tablet contains the active drug (paracetamol) plus binding agents that hold the tablet together, a coating for easy swallowing, and sometimes flavouring. The exact mass of each component is critical — too much active ingredient could be dangerous.

Paint: Contains a pigment (for colour), a solvent (to keep it liquid), a binder (to make it stick to surfaces), and additives (to control drying time or finish). Changing the proportions changes whether the paint is matt or gloss, fast-drying or slow-drying.

Chromatography

Chromatography is a powerful analytical technique used to separate mixtures of soluble substances. It can reveal whether a substance is pure or impure, and it can identify the individual components of a mixture.

Paper chromatography involves two phases. The mobile phase is the solvent (often water) that moves up through the paper. The stationary phase is the paper itself. Different substances in the mixture are carried different distances by the solvent, depending on how soluble they are. More soluble substances travel further up the paper; less soluble ones stay closer to the start line.

Step 1: Draw a pencil line 1 cm from the bottom of the chromatography paper. Use pencil, not pen, because pencil ink is insoluble and will not dissolve in the solvent.

Step 2: Place small spots of each substance onto the pencil line, leaving gaps between them so they do not merge.

Step 3: Pour a shallow layer of solvent into a beaker. The solvent level must be below the pencil line so that the spots do not dissolve directly into the solvent.

Step 4: Lower the paper into the solvent and leave it undisturbed. The solvent will travel up the paper by capillary action, carrying the dissolved substances with it.

Step 5: Remove the paper just before the solvent front reaches the top. Mark the solvent front with a pencil and allow the chromatogram to dry.

Interpreting a Chromatogram

The pattern of spots on a finished chromatogram tells you important information. A pure substance produces just one spot. An impure substance (a mixture) produces two or more spots, one for each component in the mixture.

You can identify unknown substances by comparing their spots to known reference substances run on the same chromatogram. If an unknown spot travels the same distance as a known substance, they are likely the same chemical.

Calculating Rf Values

The Rf value (retention factor) gives each substance a numerical identity in a particular solvent. It is calculated using:

Key Fact

\(R_{f} = \text{distance moved by substance} \div \text{distance moved by solvent}\). The Rf value is always between 0 and 1. Each substance has a unique Rf value in a given solvent, so Rf values can be compared to reference data to identify unknown chemicals.

Worked example: A spot of dye travels 30 mm up the paper. The solvent front travels 52 mm. Rf = 30 ÷ 52 = 0.58 (to 2 significant figures). Different compounds have different Rf values in different solvents, so the solvent used and the conditions must always be recorded.

Tests for Common Gases

You need to know the laboratory tests for four gases: hydrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide, and chlorine. Each test has a specific method and a clear positive result that you must be able to recall.

Hydrogen: Hold a burning splint at the mouth of a test tube containing the gas. If hydrogen is present, it burns rapidly with a squeaky pop sound. Hydrogen is produced when metals react with acids (e.g. magnesium + hydrochloric acid).

Oxygen: Insert a glowing splint into a test tube of the gas. If oxygen is present, the splint relights. Oxygen can be produced by decomposing hydrogen peroxide with a manganese dioxide catalyst.

Carbon dioxide: Bubble the gas through limewater (calcium hydroxide solution). If carbon dioxide is present, the limewater turns cloudy (milky white). This happens because calcium carbonate, an insoluble white solid, is formed. Carbon dioxide is produced when carbonates react with acids.

Chlorine: Hold a piece of damp litmus paper near the gas. If chlorine is present, the litmus paper is bleached white. This happens because chlorine dissolves in the water on the damp paper and acts as a bleaching agent.

Key Fact

Remember the four gas tests: Hydrogen → squeaky pop with a burning splint. Oxygen → relights a glowing splint. Carbon dioxide → turns limewater cloudy. Chlorine → bleaches damp litmus paper white.

Students often confuse the hydrogen and oxygen tests. For hydrogen, the splint must be burning (lit). For oxygen, the splint must be glowing (no flame, just an ember). Saying “the splint relights” when testing for hydrogen, or “a squeaky pop” when testing for oxygen, will lose you marks.

Another common error is stating that carbon dioxide “extinguishes a flame.” While this is true, it is not the correct test — many gases will extinguish a flame. The specific test is the limewater test. Similarly, for chlorine, the litmus paper must be damp, not dry.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In chromatography questions, always show your Rf calculation with the formula and your working — the method mark is often awarded even if your final answer is wrong. For gas test questions, be precise: state the exact test method and the positive result. “Use a burning splint” alone is not enough for hydrogen — you must also state “a squeaky pop is heard.” For extended response questions on purity, link your answer to melting and boiling point data.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A chemically pure substance contains only one element or compound and has a sharp, specific melting and boiling point. A formulation is a mixture designed with precise proportions for a specific purpose.
  • Chromatography separates soluble substances using a mobile phase (solvent) and a stationary phase (paper). Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent. Pure substances produce one spot; mixtures produce multiple spots.
  • Know the four gas tests: hydrogen (squeaky pop), oxygen (relights glowing splint), carbon dioxide (turns limewater cloudy), chlorine (bleaches damp litmus paper white).

lessons.title: The Earth's Atmosphere and Greenhouse Effect
lessons.description: How the atmosphere evolved, what greenhouse gases do, and the human impact on climate change.
lessons.content_html:
The Earth’s Early Atmosphere

Scientists believe that for the first billion years of Earth’s existence, the atmosphere was very different from what it is today. Evidence suggests that the atmosphere was formed by volcanic degassing — the release of gases from volcanoes during intense volcanic activity. The early atmosphere was probably similar to that of Mars and Venus today.

The early atmosphere likely contained:

  • A large amount of carbon dioxide (CO₂)
  • Water vapour, which later condensed to form the oceans
  • Small amounts of methane (CH₄) and ammonia (NH₃)
  • Little or no oxygen
Key Fact

The early atmosphere was mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen. Volcanoes released carbon dioxide, water vapour, nitrogen, and small amounts of methane and ammonia. This is supported by evidence from the atmospheres of Mars and Venus, which are still mostly CO₂ today.

How Did Oxygen Appear?

Around 2.7 billion years ago, the first organisms capable of photosynthesis evolved — simple algae and cyanobacteria. These organisms used carbon dioxide and water in the presence of sunlight to produce glucose and release oxygen as a waste product.

Over hundreds of millions of years, photosynthesising organisms gradually increased the proportion of oxygen in the atmosphere. As oxygen levels rose, more complex life forms could evolve. Eventually, atmospheric oxygen reached today’s level of approximately 21%.

Carbon dioxide was removed from the early atmosphere by three main processes:

1. Photosynthesis: Algae and plants absorbed CO₂ from the atmosphere and released O₂. This was the single biggest factor in reducing atmospheric carbon dioxide.

2. Dissolving in the oceans: When the water vapour in the atmosphere condensed to form the oceans, CO₂ dissolved in the water. Some of this dissolved CO₂ formed insoluble carbonate precipitates that fell to the ocean floor and became sedimentary rocks such as limestone (CaCO₃).

3. Formation of fossil fuels: The remains of organisms that could not decay were buried under layers of sediment and, over millions of years, became fossil fuels — coal, oil, and natural gas. The carbon in these organisms originally came from atmospheric CO₂ absorbed during photosynthesis.

Today’s Atmosphere

The proportions of gases in today’s atmosphere have been broadly stable for around 200 million years. The current composition is approximately:

  • Nitrogen — about 78%
  • Oxygen — about 21%
  • Argon — about 0.9%
  • Carbon dioxide — about 0.04%
  • Small amounts of water vapour and other gases
Key Fact

Today’s atmosphere is approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and 0.9% argon, with about 0.04% carbon dioxide. These proportions have been roughly stable for the last 200 million years.

The Greenhouse Effect

The greenhouse effect is a natural process that keeps the Earth warm enough to support life. Without it, the average surface temperature would be about −18°C instead of the current average of approximately +15°C.

The process works as follows:

  • Step 1: Short-wavelength radiation from the Sun passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth’s surface.
  • Step 2: The warm surface re-emits energy as long-wavelength infrared radiation.
  • Step 3: Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere absorb some of this infrared radiation and re-emit it in all directions, including back towards the Earth’s surface.
  • Step 4: This keeps the Earth warmer than it would otherwise be.

Carbon dioxide (CO₂): Released by burning fossil fuels, deforestation, and respiration. It is the greenhouse gas most affected by human activity.

Methane (CH₄): Released by livestock farming (digestion in cattle), rice paddy fields, decomposition of waste in landfill sites, and extraction of fossil fuels. Methane is a more potent greenhouse gas than CO₂ but is present in much smaller quantities.

Water vapour (H₂O): The most abundant greenhouse gas. As temperatures rise, more water evaporates, which can amplify the greenhouse effect further.

Human Activities and Climate Change

Since the Industrial Revolution (from around 1750), human activities have released increasing amounts of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. The concentration of CO₂ has risen from about 280 parts per million (ppm) to over 420 ppm today. Most scientists agree that this rise is the main cause of recent climate change.

The main human activities responsible include:

  • Burning fossil fuels — for transport, electricity generation, heating, and industry. This releases CO₂ that was locked away millions of years ago.
  • Deforestation — cutting down forests removes trees that would absorb CO₂ through photosynthesis. Burning or decay of the wood releases the stored carbon back into the atmosphere.
  • Agriculture — rice paddies and livestock produce methane. Using nitrogen-based fertilisers releases nitrous oxide, another greenhouse gas.
  • Landfill — decomposing organic waste in landfill produces methane.
Key Fact

Since the Industrial Revolution, atmospheric CO₂ has risen from about 280 ppm to over 420 ppm. The main causes are burning fossil fuels, deforestation, agriculture, and landfill. Most scientists attribute recent climate change to this increase in greenhouse gas concentrations.

Consequences of Climate Change

Increasing global temperatures have a range of potential consequences. These include:

  • Rising sea levels caused by thermal expansion of water and melting of polar ice caps and glaciers, leading to flooding of low-lying areas.
  • More extreme weather events — more frequent and severe storms, droughts, and heatwaves.
  • Changes to ecosystems — shifts in habitats and migration patterns, loss of biodiversity, and coral bleaching in warmer oceans.
  • Food security — changing rainfall patterns and higher temperatures can reduce crop yields in some regions.

The vast majority of climate scientists agree that human activities are the main cause of recent climate change. However, some people question the extent of the human contribution. This is partly because:

• The climate has changed naturally throughout Earth’s history due to volcanic eruptions, changes in the Sun’s output, and orbital variations.

• Climate models involve complex calculations with many variables, and predictions for the future carry a degree of uncertainty.

• Economic interests — industries that depend on fossil fuels may resist policy changes that could affect profits.

Despite these debates, the scientific consensus, supported by bodies such as the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), is very strong: human activity is the dominant cause of the warming observed since the mid-20th century.

Carbon Footprint

A carbon footprint is the total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle of a product, service, or event. It is usually expressed as tonnes of CO₂ equivalent.

The carbon footprint can be reduced by actions such as:

  • Using renewable energy sources (wind, solar, hydroelectric) instead of fossil fuels.
  • Improving energy efficiency in homes and industry — insulation, LED lighting, efficient boilers.
  • Reducing, reusing, and recycling materials to cut the energy used in manufacturing.
  • Using public transport, cycling, or electric vehicles instead of petrol or diesel cars.
  • Carbon capture and storage (CCS) — capturing CO₂ from power stations before it enters the atmosphere and storing it underground.

Reducing carbon footprints is not straightforward. There are several challenges:

• Cost: Renewable energy infrastructure and carbon capture technology require significant investment.

• International cooperation: Climate change is a global issue, so action by one country alone has limited effect. Agreements like the Paris Agreement (2015) aim to coordinate international efforts, but compliance varies.

• Lifestyle changes: Many people are unwilling or unable to change habits such as driving, flying, or consuming energy-intensive products.

• Developing nations: Countries experiencing industrial growth may prioritise economic development over emission reductions, arguing that wealthier nations should lead.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In 6-mark extended response questions on this topic, make sure you write about specific gases (carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour) rather than just saying “greenhouse gases.” Always link human activities to specific consequences — for example, “burning fossil fuels releases CO₂, which increases the greenhouse effect, leading to rising global temperatures.” For questions about reducing carbon footprints, discuss both individual actions and government or industrial strategies, and evaluate their effectiveness.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The early atmosphere was mainly CO₂ with little oxygen. Photosynthesis by algae and plants increased oxygen levels and reduced CO₂ over billions of years. Today’s atmosphere is approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and 0.04% CO₂.
  • The greenhouse effect is a natural process where greenhouse gases (CO₂, methane, water vapour) absorb and re-emit infrared radiation, keeping the Earth warm. Human activities have increased greenhouse gas levels, causing enhanced global warming and climate change.
  • Carbon footprints can be reduced through renewable energy, improved efficiency, recycling, and carbon capture — but cost, international cooperation, and lifestyle changes remain significant challenges.

• Carbon capture and storage (CCS) — traps CO₂ at source, but technology is expensive and not yet widely available.
• Energy efficiency (insulation, LED lighting) — reduces energy demand and saves money long-term, but requires upfront investment.
• Electric vehicles / public transport — reduce transport emissions, but electricity must come from low-carbon sources for the benefit to be realised.
• Reducing deforestation / planting trees — trees absorb CO₂, but this alone cannot offset all emissions from fossil fuels.
• International agreements (e.g. Paris Agreement) — coordinate global efforts, but compliance is voluntary and some major emitters may not participate fully.
• Lifestyle changes (recycling, reducing consumption) — help at an individual level, but systemic change through policy and industry is also needed.
• Conclusion: a combination of strategies at individual, national, and international levels is needed because no single method can solve the problem alone.

lessons.title: Atmospheric Pollutants and Their Effects
lessons.description: Sources and effects of carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and particulates.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Atmospheric Pollutants?

When we burn fossil fuels such as coal, oil and natural gas, they don’t just produce carbon dioxide and water. Depending on the conditions and the fuel itself, a range of harmful pollutants can be released into the atmosphere. These pollutants cause serious problems for human health and the environment.

The main atmospheric pollutants you need to know are carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and particulates. Each one is produced in a different way and causes different types of damage.

Key Fact

The four atmospheric pollutants you must know for AQA are: carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2), nitrogen oxides (NOx) and particulates (soot and unburnt hydrocarbons).

Complete and Incomplete Combustion

To understand where pollutants come from, you first need to understand the difference between complete combustion and incomplete combustion.

In complete combustion, a hydrocarbon fuel burns in a plentiful supply of oxygen. The only products are carbon dioxide and water. For example, methane burning completely:

\(methane + oxygen \rightarrow \text{carbon dioxide} + water\)
CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O

In incomplete combustion, there is not enough oxygen for the fuel to burn fully. Instead of carbon dioxide, the products include carbon monoxide (CO) and particulate carbon (soot). This is what happens inside a Bunsen burner when the air hole is closed — you see a yellow, smoky flame because carbon particles glow in the heat.

\(methane + oxygen \rightarrow \text{carbon monoxide} + water\)
2CH4 + 3O2 → 2CO + 4H2O

If even less oxygen is available, solid carbon (soot) is produced as well:

\(methane + oxygen \rightarrow carbon + water\)
CH4 + O2 → C + 2H2O

Incomplete combustion occurs when there is a limited supply of oxygen. This commonly happens in car engines (especially diesel engines), gas boilers that are poorly maintained, and any enclosed space where air flow is restricted. The larger the hydrocarbon molecule, the more oxygen it needs to burn completely — which is why diesel fuel (with bigger molecules than petrol) is more likely to undergo incomplete combustion and produce particulates.

Carbon Monoxide (CO)

carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless gas, which makes it extremely dangerous because you cannot detect it without a special alarm. It is produced by the incomplete combustion of any fuel containing carbon.

Carbon monoxide is toxic because it binds to the haemoglobin in red blood cells. Haemoglobin normally carries oxygen from the lungs to the body’s tissues. Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen does, so it takes the place of oxygen molecules. This means less oxygen is carried around the body, which can lead to dizziness, unconsciousness and even death at high concentrations.

Key Fact

Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it is colourless and odourless, and it binds to haemoglobin in red blood cells, reducing the amount of oxygen the blood can carry.

Sulfur Dioxide (SO2)

sulfur dioxide is produced when fossil fuels that contain sulfur impurities are burned. Coal is particularly high in sulfur. The sulfur reacts with oxygen during combustion:

\(sulfur + oxygen \rightarrow \text{sulfur dioxide}\)
S + O2 → SO2

Sulfur dioxide can also be released naturally by volcanic eruptions. Once in the atmosphere, it dissolves in rainwater to form acid rain (sulfurous acid or sulfuric acid):

\(SO_{2} + H_{2}O \rightarrow H_{2}SO_{3}\) (sulfurous acid)

Acid rain causes widespread environmental damage. It corrodes limestone and marble buildings and statues because these are made of calcium carbonate, which reacts with acid. It kills trees by damaging their leaves and leaching minerals from the soil. It also lowers the pH of lakes and rivers, killing fish and other aquatic organisms. Acid rain can travel hundreds of kilometres from the source of the pollution, meaning one country’s emissions can damage another country’s environment.

Nitrogen Oxides (NOx)

nitrogen oxides (written as NOx) are formed when the temperature inside an engine or furnace is high enough for nitrogen and oxygen in the air to react together. This does not come from the fuel itself — it comes from the atmosphere. Car engines, aeroplane engines and power stations all produce nitrogen oxides.

Nitrogen oxides also occur naturally during lightning strikes, where the extreme heat forces nitrogen and oxygen molecules to combine. However, the vast majority of nitrogen oxides in the atmosphere come from vehicle engines.

Nitrogen oxides cause several problems. Like sulfur dioxide, they dissolve in rainwater to form acid rain. They can also trigger asthma attacks and other respiratory problems. In sunlight, nitrogen oxides react with other pollutants to form photochemical smog, which is a serious health hazard in cities.

Key Fact

Nitrogen oxides are not produced from the fuel — they form when nitrogen and oxygen from the air react at the very high temperatures inside engines. They cause acid rain, trigger asthma and contribute to smog.

Particulates

particulates are tiny solid particles released during incomplete combustion. They consist of carbon (soot) and unburnt hydrocarbons. Diesel engines are a major source because diesel molecules are larger than petrol molecules and need more oxygen to burn completely.

Particulates cause two main types of harm:

Health effects: Particulates are so small that they can penetrate deep into the lungs and even pass across cell membranes into the bloodstream. They worsen respiratory conditions like asthma and bronchitis, and long-term exposure may increase the risk of lung cancer and heart disease.

Environmental effects: When particulates travel high into the atmosphere, they reflect sunlight back into space before it reaches the Earth’s surface. This effect is called global dimming. Some scientists have suggested that global dimming may partially offset the warming effect of greenhouse gases, but it also reduces the light available for photosynthesis and can disrupt weather patterns.

Several methods can reduce the release of atmospheric pollutants. Catalytic converters in car exhausts convert carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides into less harmful carbon dioxide and nitrogen. Flue gas desulfurisation in power stations removes sulfur dioxide from waste gases before they leave the chimney. Using cleaner fuels (such as natural gas instead of coal) or renewable energy sources avoids producing these pollutants altogether. Regular maintenance of boilers and engines ensures more complete combustion, reducing carbon monoxide and particulate emissions.

Carbon monoxide (CO): From incomplete combustion. Colourless, odourless. Binds to haemoglobin, reducing oxygen transport in blood.

\(Sulfur dioxide (SO_{2}):\) From burning fuels containing sulfur. Causes acid rain, damages buildings and kills aquatic life.

\(Nitrogen oxides (NO_{x}):\) From high-temperature reactions of N2 and O2 in engines. Cause acid rain, trigger asthma, form smog.

Particulates: Soot and unburnt hydrocarbons from incomplete combustion. Cause respiratory disease and global dimming.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In questions about atmospheric pollutants, always be specific about which pollutant causes which problem — examiners will not give marks for vague answers like “pollution damages the environment.” State the pollutant by name (e.g. sulfur dioxide), explain how it is produced (burning fuels containing sulfur), and describe its specific effect (dissolves in rainwater to form acid rain, which damages limestone buildings and kills aquatic life). For 6-mark extended response questions, link the source, the pollutant and the effect in a clear chain of reasoning.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Incomplete combustion (limited oxygen) produces carbon monoxide and particulates, while complete combustion produces only carbon dioxide and water.
  • Carbon monoxide is toxic because it binds to haemoglobin, reducing the blood’s ability to carry oxygen.
  • Sulfur dioxide (from sulfur impurities in fuel) and nitrogen oxides (from high-temperature reactions in engines) both cause acid rain, while particulates cause global dimming and respiratory health problems.

lessons.title: Using Earth's Resources and Sustainability
lessons.description: Natural resources, potable water, life cycle assessments, and sustainable resource use.
lessons.content_html:
Using Earth’s Natural Resources

Humans rely on the Earth’s natural resources to survive and develop. Some of these resources are finite — they will eventually run out because they are being used faster than they can be replaced. Fossil fuels and metal ores are finite resources. Others are renewable, meaning they can be replaced at the same rate they are used, such as timber from managed forests.

Chemistry plays a key role in improving the way we use natural resources. For example, agriculture uses synthetic fertilisers to improve crop yields, and industry develops new materials like polymers and alloys from Earth’s raw materials. The challenge is to do this sustainably — meeting our needs today without preventing future generations from meeting theirs.

Key Fact

Natural resources can be classified as finite (non-renewable — will run out) or renewable (can be replaced). Sustainable development means using resources at a rate that does not compromise future availability.

Potable Water

Potable water is water that is safe to drink. It is not the same as pure water — potable water still contains dissolved substances, but at levels that are not harmful. In the UK, most potable water comes from surface water sources such as rivers and reservoirs.

Making water potable in the UK involves three main stages:

1. Filtration — Water passes through filter beds made of sand and gravel. This removes large particles such as leaves, soil, and debris.

2. Sedimentation — Chemicals are added that cause fine particles to clump together and sink to the bottom, forming a sediment that can be removed.

3. Sterilisation — The water is treated with chlorine, ozone, or ultraviolet light to kill harmful bacteria and other microbes. This makes the water safe to drink.

In some countries where fresh water is scarce, desalination is used to produce potable water from seawater. This can be done by distillation (boiling and condensing) or by reverse osmosis (forcing water through membranes that filter out salt ions). Both methods require large amounts of energy, making desalination expensive.

Waste Water Treatment

Water that has been used in homes, agriculture, and industry becomes waste water. Domestic waste water includes sewage from toilets, sinks, and showers. Industrial and agricultural waste water may contain harmful chemicals, heavy metals, or organic waste.

Waste water must be treated before being released back into the environment to prevent pollution and the spread of disease. Treatment involves several stages:

Screening — Large objects such as rags and plastic are removed using metal grilles.

Sedimentation — The sewage is held in large tanks where solid material settles as sludge. The liquid effluent is separated off.

Anaerobic digestion of sludge — The sludge is broken down by bacteria in the absence of oxygen. This produces biogas (mainly methane), which can be used as a fuel, and a solid residue that can be used as fertiliser.

Aerobic treatment of effluent — The liquid effluent is treated with aerobic bacteria (in the presence of oxygen) to break down remaining organic matter. The treated water is then safe to release into rivers or the sea.

Life Cycle Assessments

A life cycle assessment (LCA) examines the environmental impact of a product at every stage of its life — from “cradle to grave.” This helps companies and consumers make informed choices about which products are more environmentally friendly.

The four stages of an LCA are:

Stage 1

Extracting Raw Materials

Mining ores, drilling for oil, or harvesting crops. Considers energy used, land damage, and water consumption.

Stage 2

Manufacturing & Processing

Turning raw materials into the product. Considers energy input, waste produced, and pollutants released.

Stage 3

Use & Distribution

Transporting the product to consumers and energy used during its lifetime (e.g. fuel for a car, electricity for a phone).

Stage 4

Disposal

What happens at end of life — landfill, incineration, or recycling. Each has a different environmental cost.

Key Fact

LCAs can be subjective — some environmental impacts (like the effect on local wildlife) are difficult to measure and involve value judgements. This means different LCAs of the same product can reach different conclusions depending on what is prioritised.

Reducing Our Impact — The Three Rs

The simplest way to reduce the environmental impact of products is to follow the three Rs: reduce, reuse, recycle. Reducing means using fewer resources in the first place. Reusing means finding new purposes for products instead of discarding them. Recycling means processing waste materials into new products.

Recycling metals is particularly important. Extracting metals from ores requires large amounts of energy (usually from fossil fuels) and produces waste rock and toxic gases. Recycling aluminium, for example, uses only about 5% of the energy needed to extract it from bauxite ore.

Extracting Metals from Low-Grade Ores

As high-grade metal ores become scarce, scientists have developed new methods to extract metals from low-grade ores and even from waste. Two key biological methods are phytomining and bioleaching.

Phytomining: Certain plants are grown on land that contains low concentrations of metal compounds. The plants absorb the metal ions through their roots and accumulate them in their tissues. The plants are then harvested and burned. The ash contains a higher concentration of metal, which can be extracted by smelting or electrolysis.

Bioleaching: Bacteria are used to break down low-grade ores. The bacteria produce an acidic solution called a leachate, which contains dissolved metal compounds. The metal can then be extracted from this solution, often by displacement using a more reactive metal or by electrolysis.

Both methods are slower than traditional mining but are more environmentally friendly because they do not require huge amounts of energy or produce large volumes of waste rock.

Key Fact

Phytomining uses plants to absorb metals from soil; bioleaching uses bacteria to dissolve metals from low-grade ores. Both are sustainable alternatives to traditional mining for extracting copper and other metals.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on this topic often ask you to compare methods (e.g. desalination vs. filtration, phytomining vs. bioleaching) or evaluate the use of LCAs. Remember that LCAs involve subjective judgements — always explain why some data is hard to quantify. For 6-mark extended responses, use a clear structure: state a point, explain the science, then link it to the environmental or economic impact.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Natural resources are either finite (e.g. fossil fuels, ores) or renewable (e.g. timber). Sustainable development means using resources without compromising future supply.
  • Potable water is made safe by filtration, sedimentation, and sterilisation. In water-scarce areas, desalination of seawater is used but requires significant energy.
  • Life cycle assessments analyse a product’s environmental impact from cradle to grave, but some impacts are difficult to measure objectively. Reduce, reuse, and recycle are the simplest ways to lower environmental impact.

lessons.title: Alkenes, Alcohols and Carboxylic Acids
lessons.description: The structure and reactions of alkenes, alcohols and carboxylic acids as functional group chemistry.
lessons.content_html:
Functional Groups

Organic chemistry is the study of carbon compounds. Carbon atoms can form four covalent bonds, which allows them to build chains and rings of almost unlimited size. The properties of an organic molecule depend on its functional group — the specific atom or group of atoms within the molecule that controls how it reacts. Alkenes, alcohols, and carboxylic acids are three important homologous series, each defined by a different functional group.

Alkenes

Alkenes are hydrocarbons that contain at least one carbon–carbon double bond (C=C). This double bond is their functional group. The general formula for alkenes is CₙH₂ₙ, where n is the number of carbon atoms. The simplest alkene is ethene (C₂H₄), followed by propene (C₃H₆) and butene (C₄H₈).

Key Fact

Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons because they contain a C=C double bond. Alkanes are saturated because they contain only single C–C bonds. This single difference in bonding gives the two families very different reactivity.

Because alkenes have a double bond, they are more reactive than alkanes. The double bond can “open up” and allow other atoms to add across it. This type of reaction is called an addition reaction.

Addition of hydrogen (hydrogenation): Alkenes react with hydrogen gas in the presence of a nickel catalyst at about 150 °C. The hydrogen atoms add across the double bond, converting the alkene into an alkane. For example: ethene + hydrogen → ethane (C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆). This reaction is used industrially to harden vegetable oils into margarine.

Addition of water (hydration): Alkenes react with steam in the presence of a phosphoric acid catalyst at high temperature and pressure. This produces an alcohol. For example: ethene + steam → ethanol (C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH). This is the industrial method for making ethanol.

Addition of halogens: Alkenes react rapidly with halogens such as bromine. Ethene decolourises bromine water from orange to colourless, forming a colourless dibromo compound. This is the standard test to distinguish alkenes from alkanes — alkanes do not decolourise bromine water because they have no double bond to react with.

Key Fact

Test for alkenes: Shake the substance with bromine water. If the bromine water changes from orange to colourless, the substance is an alkene (unsaturated). If it stays orange, the substance is saturated (an alkane).

Alcohols

Alcohols are a homologous series of organic compounds whose functional group is the hydroxyl group (–OH). The general formula for alcohols is CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH. The first four members are methanol (CH₃OH), ethanol (C₂H₅OH), propanol (C₃H₇OH), and butanol (C₄H₉OH).

Alcohols dissolve in water to form neutral solutions — they do not produce H⁺ ions, so they are not acidic. They react with sodium metal to produce hydrogen gas and a sodium alkoxide. Alcohols also burn in air, releasing energy, which makes them useful as fuels. Ethanol is the alcohol in alcoholic drinks and is widely used as a solvent and as a fuel (often blended with petrol).

There are two ways to make ethanol on an industrial scale:

Hydration of ethene: Ethene (from cracking crude oil) reacts with steam using a phosphoric acid catalyst at 300 °C and 60–70 atm. This is a continuous process that produces pure ethanol quickly, but it uses a non-renewable feedstock (crude oil).

Fermentation: Yeast converts sugars (e.g. glucose from crops) into ethanol and carbon dioxide at about 25–35 °C in the absence of oxygen: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide (C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂). Fermentation uses a renewable feedstock (sugar from plants) and requires low temperatures, so energy costs are low. However, the process is slow (batch process), and the ethanol produced is impure — it must be separated from the mixture by fractional distillation.

Key Fact

Hydration of ethene is faster and gives purer ethanol but uses a non-renewable feedstock. Fermentation is slower and gives impure ethanol but uses a renewable feedstock and lower temperatures. Exam questions often ask you to compare these two methods.

Carboxylic Acids

Carboxylic acids contain the functional group –COOH (also written as –CO₂H). This group contains both a C=O double bond and an O–H bond. The first members of the series are methanoic acid (HCOOH), ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH — found in vinegar), propanoic acid, and butanoic acid.

Carboxylic acids dissolve in water to produce weak acidic solutions. They ionise only partially — only a small proportion of the acid molecules release H⁺ ions at any one time. This means a solution of ethanoic acid has a higher pH (is less acidic) than a solution of hydrochloric acid of the same concentration.

Carboxylic acids show the typical reactions of acids, but they react more slowly because they are weak acids:

With metal carbonates: Carboxylic acids react with carbonates to produce a salt, water, and carbon dioxide. For example: ethanoic acid + sodium carbonate → sodium ethanoate + water + carbon dioxide (2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂).

With water: Carboxylic acids dissolve in water and partially dissociate, producing H⁺ ions. The solution is acidic but weakly so.

With alcohols: Carboxylic acids react with alcohols in the presence of an acid catalyst to form esters. For example: ethanoic acid + ethanol → ethyl ethanoate + water. Esters often have pleasant, fruity smells and are used in flavourings, perfumes, and solvents.

Strong acids (e.g. hydrochloric acid, sulfuric acid) completely ionise in water — every acid molecule releases H⁺ ions. Weak acids (e.g. ethanoic acid, citric acid) only partially ionise — most of the acid molecules remain intact in solution. At the same concentration, a strong acid has a lower pH, reacts faster, and conducts electricity better than a weak acid because it has a higher concentration of H⁺ ions.

Do not confuse acid strength with concentration. Strength refers to the degree of ionisation. Concentration refers to how much acid is dissolved per unit volume of solution. A concentrated weak acid (e.g. concentrated ethanoic acid) can still have a higher pH than a dilute strong acid.

Key Fact

Carboxylic acids are weak acids because they only partially ionise in water. At the same concentration, ethanoic acid has a higher pH, reacts more slowly, and produces less gas with carbonates than hydrochloric acid (a strong acid).

lessons.title: Polymers: Addition, Condensation and Natural
lessons.description: Addition and condensation polymerisation, amino acids, and natural polymers like DNA.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Polymers?

A polymer is a very large molecule formed when many small molecules called monomers bond together in a repeating pattern. The word “polymer” comes from the Greek for “many parts.” Polymers can be synthetic (made by humans) or naturally occurring. Everyday synthetic polymers include poly(ethene), PVC, and PTFE, while natural polymers include proteins, starch, and DNA.

The process of joining monomers together is called polymerisation. There are two main types of polymerisation you need to know for GCSE Chemistry: addition polymerisation and condensation polymerisation. Each works in a different way and produces a different type of polymer.

Addition Polymerisation

addition polymerisation occurs when many unsaturated monomer molecules (alkenes) join together. The carbon–carbon double bond (C=C) in each monomer “opens up,” allowing the monomers to link into a long chain. No other substance is produced — the only product is the polymer itself.

The simplest example is poly(ethene). Ethene (C₂H₄) is the monomer. Under high pressure and with a catalyst, thousands of ethene molecules open their double bonds and bond together to form a long-chain polymer. The repeating unit of poly(ethene) looks the same as the monomer but with single bonds on each side instead of a double bond.

Key Fact

In addition polymerisation, the only product is the polymer. No atoms are lost or gained — the polymer has the same empirical formula as the monomer. The letter n in the equation represents a very large number of monomer molecules joining together.

To show addition polymerisation in an equation, write n monomer molecules on the left with the C=C double bond shown. On the right, draw the repeating unit inside brackets with a single bond extending from each side of the bracket. Place n as a subscript outside the brackets. The key change: the double bond in the monomer becomes a single bond in the polymer.

Common examples include poly(propene) from propene, and poly(chloroethene) — better known as PVC — from chloroethene. In each case, identify the alkene monomer, open the double bond, and extend the chain. Exam questions often ask you to draw the repeating unit given the monomer, or to identify the monomer from the polymer.

Condensation Polymerisation

condensation polymerisation is different from addition polymerisation in two important ways. First, the monomers have two functional groups — one on each end of the molecule. Second, a small molecule (usually water) is released every time two monomers join together. This by-product is the reason it is called “condensation” polymerisation.

Condensation polymers include polyesters and polyamides. To form a polyester, a dicarboxylic acid reacts with a diol. The –COOH group on the acid reacts with the –OH group on the alcohol, forming an ester link (–COO–) and releasing a molecule of water (H₂O) each time.

Key Fact

The crucial difference: addition polymerisation produces only the polymer, while condensation polymerisation produces the polymer and a small molecule by-product (usually water). This is the most common comparison question in the exam.

A polyamide forms when a dicarboxylic acid reacts with a diamine. The –COOH group reacts with the –NH₂ group, forming an amide link (–CONH–) and releasing water. Nylon is a well-known synthetic polyamide.

amino acids are special monomers because each molecule contains both an amine group (–NH₂) and a carboxylic acid group (–COOH). This means amino acids can undergo condensation polymerisation with each other. When two amino acids join, a peptide bond forms (a type of amide link) and water is released. Chains of amino acids form polypeptides, and one or more polypeptides fold into a protein.

Naturally Occurring Polymers

Many of the most important molecules in living organisms are polymers. You need to know three key examples for the exam: proteins, starch, and DNA. Each is built from smaller monomer units through condensation polymerisation.

Proteins are natural polyamides. They are condensation polymers of amino acids linked by peptide bonds. There are 20 different amino acids found in nature, and the order in which they join determines the protein’s shape and function. Proteins act as enzymes, hormones, antibodies, and structural materials such as collagen and keratin.

starch is a natural polymer made from glucose monomers joined together by condensation reactions. Plants produce starch to store energy. Cellulose is another glucose-based polymer, but the glucose units are arranged differently, giving cellulose rigid, structural properties. Both starch and cellulose release water molecules when their monomers join.

DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a polymer made from nucleotide monomers. Each nucleotide contains a sugar, a phosphate group, and a base. Nucleotides join by condensation reactions to form the two strands of the DNA double helix. The sequence of bases along the strand carries the genetic instructions for building proteins.

Key Fact

All three naturally occurring polymers — proteins, starch, and DNA — are formed by condensation polymerisation. In every case, monomers join together and water molecules are released as by-products.

Comparing the Two Types of Polymerisation

Exam questions frequently ask you to compare addition and condensation polymerisation. The table below summarises the key differences.

Addition polymerisation: monomers are alkenes with C=C double bonds; only one product (the polymer); no by-product; examples include poly(ethene), poly(propene), PVC. Condensation polymerisation: monomers have two functional groups (e.g. –OH and –COOH); two products (the polymer and a small molecule, usually water); examples include polyesters, nylon, proteins, starch, DNA.

Question: A polymer is formed from monomers with two different functional groups. Water is also produced. What type of polymerisation is this?

Answer: This is condensation polymerisation. The clues are: (1) the monomers have two functional groups, not a C=C double bond, and (2) a small molecule (water) is produced as a by-product. In addition polymerisation, there is no by-product — only the polymer is formed.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The most common exam question on this topic asks you to compare addition and condensation polymerisation. Always state three differences: (1) the type of monomer used, (2) whether a by-product is formed, and (3) give a named example of each. For 6-mark extended response questions, link your answer to naturally occurring polymers such as proteins and DNA to show breadth of knowledge. Remember — if water is produced, it is condensation polymerisation.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Addition polymerisation joins alkene monomers by opening C=C double bonds, producing only the polymer with no by-product.
  • Condensation polymerisation joins monomers with two functional groups, producing the polymer and a small molecule (usually water).
  • Proteins (from amino acids), starch (from glucose), and DNA (from nucleotides) are all naturally occurring condensation polymers.
